‘ 8 / y!l‘ © Grammar Focus \4:,+ W/ * Reported Speech — ; ) When we tell someone what another person said, we usually do / not repeat their exact words, Instead, we report the idea using !/ reported speech. This is especially useful for reporting the 4 opinion of conservationists A reported sentence usually begins with a reporting verb such as “said, told . explained. added. replied. or claimed” followed by (that) and a clausc. The word “that™ is optional and is often
dropped in spoken English.
Subject + said (that) + clause
The farmer said (that) he needed more land.
Subject + told + person + (that) + clause
The farmer told the officer (that) he needed more land.
Note the difference: say is not followed directly by a person (say to somebody). while fell must be followed by a person (tell somebody)
Changing the Tense
When the reporting verb is in the past (said, told, explained ..), the verb in the reported clause usually moves “one step back™ into the past. This is called backshift.
» Note : Remember 1o change pronouns and time/place expressions when needed (e.g. “today” — “that day”).
Changing Pronouns and Possessives
Because we are now speaking about the person, not as the person, pronouns and possessive adjectives usually change to match the point of view of the reporter.
When we report a question, we change the word order of the
question to statement order.
We make changes to the tenses and other words for reported
statements.

pages.topic: increasing the risk of extinction over time.

blocks.text: One of the greatest threats to wildlife today is habitat fragmentation. As cities expand, forests are cleared, roads are built, and farmland extends into natural areas. These
developments divide large ccosystems into smaller sections, making it difficult for
animals to find mates, hunt for food, or escape the effects of environmental changes.
Species that once traveled freely may become isolated. reducing genetic diversity and increasing the risk of extinction over time.

To address this problem, conservationists have developed wildlife corridors. These are protected strips of land that connect separated habitats, allowing animals to move safely between them. Some cornidors follow rivers or mountain ranges, while others include specially designed bridges or tunnels that allow animals to cross busy highways.
Such projects have already helped protect species including elephants, wolves, deer, and large cats in different parts of the world.

Nevertheless, wildlife corridors sometimes create disagreements. Farmers may worry that wild animals will damage crops or threaten livestock. Developers may argue that conservation projects reduce the amount of land available for housing or industry.

Governments therefore face the challenge of balancing environmental protection with economic development. Successful solutions usually involve careful planning, scientific research, and cooperation among local communities, businesses, and environmental organizations.

Technology has also become an important tool for protecting shared spaces. Scientists now use satellite tracking, motion-sensitive cameras, and drones to monitor animal movements. The information collected helps researchers understand migration patterns and identify the safest locations for new wildlife corridors. As climate change continues 10 alter ecosystems, this information is becoming increasingly valuable for furure

pages.plainText:
One of the greatest threats to wildlife today is habitat fragmentation. As cities expand,
forests are cleared, roads are built, and farmland extends into natural areas. These
developments divide large ccosystems into smaller sections, making it difficult for
animals to find mates, hunt for food, or escape the effects of environmental changes.
Species that once traveled freely may become isolated. reducing genetic diversity and
increasing the risk of extinction over time.
To address this problem, conservationists have developed wildlife corridors. These
are protected strips of land that connect separated habitats, allowing animals to move
safely between them. Some cornidors follow rivers or mountain ranges, while others
include specially designed bridges or tunnels that allow animals to cross busy highways.
Such projects have already helped protect species including elephants, wolves, deer, and
large cats in different parts of the world.
Nevertheless, wildlife corridors sometimes create disagreements. Farmers may
worry that wild animals will damage crops or threaten livestock. Developers may argue
that conservation projects reduce the amount of land available for housing or industry.
Governments therefore face the challenge of balancing environmental protection with
economic development. Successful solutions usually involve careful planning, scientific
research, and cooperation among local communities, businesses, and environmental
organizations.
Technology has also become an important tool for protecting shared spaces. Scientists
now use satellite tracking, motion-sensitive cameras, and drones to monitor animal
movements. The information collected helps researchers understand migration patterns
and identify the safest locations for new wildlife corridors. As climate change continues
10 alter ecosystems, this information is becoming increasingly valuable for furure
conservation planning.

From a Hobby to a Future Path
At fourtcen, Omar repaired old radios at home because he enjoyed discovering why
they stopped working. He had no business plan and did not imagine that the hobby

blocks.text: would influence his future. At first, he used to work alone at a small desk, and every Friday he would test one damaged device borrowed from a relative. The activity was relaxing. but it also taught him patience. careful observation and the satisfaction of solving a real problem.

Small opportunities accumulated gradually. A neighbor asked Omar to examine a broken speaker, a teacher invited him to demonstrate a simple repair at a school fair, and several classmates began bringing him devices. Before long, he had a waiting list.

Omar realized that enthusiasm alone was not enough: he needed better organization, safe tools and people who could share the work. He mvited three friends with sinular interests, and their private hobby began to form a small community.
The turning pomt came when the school opened an after-school vocational workshop.

There, the group gained hands-on experience in electrical safety, tool use and basic design. They also learned to divide tasks. explain technical 1deas clearly and evaluate whether a repair was worth attempting. These skills mattered beyond the workshop.
Employers are increasingly looking for people who can adapt to change, communicate effectively and solve unfamiliar problems instead of simply repeating memorized information.
Omar and his friends then created a monthly Repair Circle at the local youth centre.

It was not a business: repairs were free, and no item was guaranteed to be fixed. Visitors watched the process, while younger students learned how to identify simple faults and use tools responsibly. The group did not accept every broken device; it selected a manageable number so that members could learn carefully rather than rush. The project therefore combined community service, collaborative learning and practical career
preparation.

During the first months, Omar nearly mrned the project mto another source of pressure. He accepted too many requests, stayed late and began to lose the enjoyment that had started everything. The group responded by setting clear roles and a realistic schedule. Each member practised regularly. but nobody was expecied o work for hours every day. The turning pomt came when the school opened an after-school vocational workshop.
There, the group gained hands-on experience in electrical safety, tool use and basic
design. They also learned to divide tasks. explain technical 1deas clearly and evaluate
whether a repair was worth attempting. These skills mattered beyond the workshop.
Employers are increasingly looking for people who can adapt to change, communicate
effectively and solve unfamiliar problems instead of simply repeating memorized
information.
Omar and his friends then created a monthly Repair Circle at the local youth centre.
It was not a business: repairs were free, and no item was guaranteed to be fixed. Visitors
watched the process, while younger students learned how to identify simple faults and
use tools responsibly. The group did not accept every broken device; it selected
a manageable number so that members could learn carefully rather than rush. The project
therefore combined community service, collaborative learning and practical career
preparation.

and mostly invisible chain of resources, labor, and emissions that the
price on the screen rarely reflects.

Consider the average online order. A warehouse worker locates the item, often walking many kilometers across a fulfillment center floor during a single shift, before 1t is packed mto a box sized for a much larger product simply because that size was available in stock.

Multiply this by millions of daily deliveries, and the carbon cost of “free” next-day shipping becomes cansiderable, even though no mdividual customer ever sees the exhanst from the van outside their building.

The Corner That Changed More Than Clothes

At a secondary school in Alexandria, the “Share Corner” began with one shelf outside the library. Students could leave clean uniforms, books and sports equipment that they no longer needed, and anyone could take an item without paying or exchanging something in return. The idea was suggested after a group noticed that usable belongings were being thrown away while some classmates quietly struggled to replace lost or damaged items. At first, the organizers expected the shelf to solve a

small practical problem. They did not expect it to change how students related 1o one another The project addressed more than visible waste. Every new item carries hidden costs: raw materials, factory labor, packaging, transport and emissions. Reusing a school bag does not remove all these problems, but it can reduce the demand for another purchase. To avoid making exaggerated claims, the organizers recorded the number and type of items exchanged each month. They explained that a school

project could make a measurable difference while still being too small to replace wider action by companies and governments, The strongest effect appeared in the atmosphere around the shelf. Visitors did not have to explain why they needed something, and volunteers were trained to offer help without asking personal questions. This low-pressure approach reduced embarrassment. It also gave new students a natural reason to speak to others.

Mariam, who had felt almost invisible during her first weeks at school, began by arranging books for ten minutes after class. Within a term, she was greeting visitors, training younger volunteers and describing the project during assembly.

Success also brought problems. A social media account falsely announced that the school was giving away brand-new phones, and a crowd arnved expecting expensive products. Some donated items were damaged or unsuitable, while photographs posted without context made the Share Corner appear disorganised. The team responded by correcting the nusleading post, setting clear quality rules and verifying every photograph and claim before publication. These steps protected trust and
taught students that community projects need accurate communication as much as enthusiasim.

Mariam’s teacher became an important mentor during this period. She offered encouragement but did not give empty praise. When Mariam's first presentation was unclear, the teacher helped her identify the problem and asked her to revise it, Mariam then had the posters redesigned and the donation boxes labeled more clearly. Being allowed to make mistakes, receive honest feedback and try again made 157
